doc.title: Evan Christopher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 1, 2009

title: Why he avoids the word Dixieland; early California Dixieland experiences
summary: He finds the term pejorative and tied to the Original Dixieland Jazz Band's novelty, though New York Dixielanders are heroes. He recalls transcribing Dodds and Bill Napier solos and playing hardware store openings.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: You know I have yet to hear you use the word “Dixieland.” I think.
I don’t use it very often.
And it’s a word that carries connotations with it.

And that’s why I don’t use it. I think for me it’s a pejorative term for the music that creates a lot of misunderstanding about the New Orleans tradition. Even friends of mine, colleagues of mine in New York don’t have, they don’t give me evidence they really have any understanding of New Orleans’ music, its significance to them, and they certainly don’t know any of the repertoire. But I think there’s a New York sort of Dixieland tradition that I think they understand better. And the reason I don’t use it is because historically the first time you think of Dixieland you think of the Original Dixieland Jazz Band, which to me is almost an oxymoron because it wasn’t really a jazz band. You have to remember that, yeah, these musicians were from New Orleans but they weren’t improvising musicians, not at first, not when they first came up as young men. They were playing the music as a novelty music. It was similar to the way they played the music in New Orleans. But it wasn’t really the way they played the music in New Orleans. And I think, for better or worse, the style changed. But for me, right away that connotation of the music being more for novelty doesn’t do it justice when I speak about it, so I usually do purposely avoid the word. But there are instances where I use it and I don’t mean it in a pejorative way or I mean I think, when I think of the New York Dixielanders, I mean and the cats who played at Nick’s and Condon’s and the Metropole, I mean those are some of my heroes too. Those are some of my heroes as well. And some of the first music I heard, before I really knew anything about New Orleans music were west coast Dixieland type bands. I think the first solo I ever transcribed, well there were two, the first solos that I ever transcribed were clarinet solos and one of them was Johnny Dodds “Struttin’ with some Barbeque” with Louis Armstrong’s Hot Five, and I mean I still remember [plays]. I mean that was one of the first songs. But the other solo I learned was by a clarinetist named Bill Napier, who was with the West Coast Dixieland Band, one of the trombonists named Bob Scobey. And the solo was on “Bill Bailey.” And I remember that too. [plays] I mean so I listened to a lot of those recordings and it didn’t — and in California my early experiences were probably more Dixieland-type experiences than they were New Orleans experiences, the difference being, obviously, one was a little more commercial, arrangements maybe a little bit more clever or slicker, and yeah, I mean I played hardware store openings where the band leader gave me a straw hat out of the back of his truck before I put the horn to my face. So yeah, of course, we had that. And I even subbed at Disneyland. I even subbed with a little band out there at Disneyland. Well I mean not very often but I mean so I saw that. But ironically, ironically Disneyland was the first time that I think I was conscious of how New Orleans clarinet sounded differently than Dixieland clarinet. At Disneyland there was, toward the end of the day, they’d get ready for a parade and they’d have all these speakers spaced out because the parade had a soundtrack.
